title: Israel's Gifts and God's Freedom
sum: Chapter 9 opens a new movement of the letter. After the joy at the end of chapter 8, Paul says his grief is great and his sorrow never stops: most of his own people have not believed in Jesus. He lists what God gave Israel (9:4-5) and then asks the question that hangs over chapters 9 to 11: has God's word failed? He answers that it has not. God's promise has always worked by choosing, and not everyone born into Israel is counted as Israel (9:6-13).

Paul then raises the objection that this makes God unfair (9:14). He answers with Moses and Pharaoh (9:15-18) and with the potter and the clay (9:19-24). He calls Hosea and Isaiah as witnesses that God always meant to call a people from the nations and to save a remnant of Israel (9:25-29). The chapter ends with a puzzle: Gentiles who were not chasing righteousness received it, while Israel, which chased it, tripped over the stone God set in Zion (9:30-33). Chapter 10 explains why.
readings: Read as God's choice of persons

Augustine, Luther, Calvin and the Reformed confessions read the chapter as teaching that before birth, and apart from anything done, God chooses some people for salvation and passes over others. Jacob and Esau are persons; the potter's two vessels are two kinds of people; the objection of 9:19 is the objection every hearer of this teaching raises, and Paul does not answer it by softening the teaching but by reminding the objector who God is.
Read as God's choice of peoples and roles

Wesley and many recent scholars (Dunn, Wright, Abasciano) point out that Paul's Old Testament cases concern nations and their place in history: Isaac's line, Israel and Edom, Pharaoh as a king used to show God's power. On this reading the question is not who will be saved forever but who carries God's promise and how, and the answer is that it was never fixed by birth or merit. Vessels can still be changed (Jeremiah 18; Romans 11:23).

Paul asks what any Jew would ask: if the Messiah has come and Israel has largely not received him, has God's promise to Israel failed? Read from Israel's side, the chapter is a defense of God's faithfulness. Its answer goes back to the stories every Jewish reader knew, in which the promise always passed through a chosen few (Isaac, Jacob, the seven thousand) without ever abandoning the whole.

views.H: Paul writes from Corinth in the winter of about AD 56-57, just before he takes the collection to Jerusalem, where he expects hostility (15:25-31). In Rome the Jews expelled under Claudius (about AD 49; Suetonius, Claudius 25.4; Acts 18:2) were coming back, and the Gentile believers had become the majority. Paul's grief for Israel is set beside his fear of what waits for him in Judea. The stories of Isaac, Jacob and Esau, and Pharaoh were read aloud in the synagogues where Roman Jews and God-fearers had heard them.
views.C: Chapters 9 to 11 were once treated as a side-trip in the letter; most scholars now see them as its climax, the answer to the question raised in 3:1-4 about God's faithfulness (Dunn, Moo, Wright). Paul's quotations mix the Septuagint with the Hebrew and sometimes join two passages (9:27; 9:33). The punctuation of 9:5 is a real textual question (see the variant entry). The diatribe style (Stowers) matters for 9:14-23: the speaker answers an imagined objector, and a reader who treats the potter passage as a free-standing doctrine of decrees may mishear it.
views.L: The chapter has a clear plan: lament (9:1-5), thesis (9:6a), three cases from Genesis and Exodus (Isaac, Jacob, Pharaoh), objection and answer (9:14-24), witnesses from the prophets (Hosea 9:25-26; Isaiah 9:27-29) and a summary in the words "righteousness" and "stumbling" (9:30-33). Key words repeat: call (9:7, 12, 24-26), mercy (9:15, 16, 18, 23), promise (9:4, 8, 9). Each quotation is introduced by a formula: "it is written," "Scripture says," "Isaiah cries out."
views.J: Paul begins as a Jew mourning for his people and offering to be cursed for them, as Moses once offered to be wiped out of God's book for Israel's sin (Exodus 32:32). Krister Stendahl and many Jewish readers see 9:1-5 as Paul's own evidence that he never gave up on Israel. The rabbis also felt the problem of Pharaoh: a comment in Exodus Rabbah 13:3, given in the name of Resh Lakish, says that God warns a person once, twice and three times before closing the door of repentance. Messianic Jewish and Paul-within-Judaism readers (Kinzer, Nanos) stress that nothing in the chapter says Israel has been cast off.
views.T: Chapter 9 is where the doctrine of predestination was fought out. Origen read it against Gnostics who said that some people are saved by nature. Augustine, from the time of his answer to Simplicianus (about AD 396), read 9:16 to mean that even the first move of faith is God's gift. Aquinas separated predestination to glory from the permitting of sin. Luther (The Bondage of the Will) and Calvin (Institutes 3.21-24) drew the strongest conclusions; Arminius (Analysis of Romans 9, 1593) and Wesley (Predestination Calmly Considered) answered with election in Christ and foreseen faith; Barth (Church Dogmatics II/2) rebuilt election around Christ himself. The Orthodox read the chapter inside the teaching that God and the human will work together. The cards below set these side by side.

deep.h: Isaac, Jacob and Pharaoh: three different cases
deep.b:
Paul's three examples are often treated as one argument, but they do different work. Isaac (9:7-9) shows that the promise was carried by a child of God's word, not just of Abraham's body; it concerns who counts in Abraham's family. Jacob and Esau (9:10-13) push the point back before birth: even twins of one father and one mother were treated differently before they did anything, so that God's purpose would stand "not by works but by the one who calls." The quoted word was about two nations (Genesis 25:23; Malachi 1:2-3), and Paul lets the personal names stand for the peoples. Pharaoh (9:17-18) is a different kind of case. Pharaoh is not chosen to carry a promise but is used to show God's power and name. The word "hardens" is the new thing, and the Exodus story gives a mixed order of events: in the first plagues Pharaoh's hardening is reported first (Exodus 8:15, 32), God's hardening is announced earlier (Exodus 4:21; 7:3) and reported from Exodus 9:12, and readers differ on how to count this (see the note on 9:18).

Notice what Paul does not say. He never says that Esau was damned or that Pharaoh could not have repented. He does not use the word "hell" or "eternal." The words he does use, "love," "hate," "mercy," "harden," "destruction," have to be read in the stories they come from. Readers of every tradition should keep the distinction between what Paul says and what later doctrine concludes from it.

The potter and the clay (9:19-24) is the best-known and most misused part of the chapter. Three points help. First, Paul is answering an objector in the diatribe style; the objector's question, "Why does he still find fault?", is not meant to be solved by a theory of decrees but by a reminder of who is asking. Second, the source texts in Isaiah (29:16; 45:9) are about Israel complaining to God, so the clay that talks back is Israel, not the reader's neighbor. Third, the potter in Jeremiah 18 is a potter who remakes the vessel and who changes his plan if the nation turns. Paul's question in 9:21 asks only whether the potter has the right to make different vessels; whether the vessels stay what they are is not answered there, and 11:23 says the "cut off" can be grafted in again.

The sentence in 9:22-24 does not finish: "What if God..." has no "then." The reader is invited to see what God has done: he bore with patience, he prepared mercy beforehand, and he called people from both Jews and Gentiles. That, rather than a theory of two classes, is where the paragraph ends (9:24).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the "what if" of 9:22-24 is Israel's own history
deep.b: My own suggestion, labeled as such: the "vessels of anger" God bore "with much patience" are Israel itself under judgment, for generations before the exile and then in Paul's own day, and the "vessels of mercy" are the called from both Jews and Gentiles (9:24). On this reading the line between the two vessels runs through Israel, which is why Paul passes at once to the remnant (9:27-29) and why he later says the broken-off branches can be grafted in again (11:23). The reading uses the Jeremiah 18 potter, who remakes the vessel, and takes "fitted" (9:22) as reflexive or as a divine passive for judgment on a people who had hardened themselves. It overlaps with published corporate readings, especially N. T. Wright's account of 9:22-24 as God's patience with Israel in exile. It is a guess about what Paul had in mind; the Greek allows other readings.
deep.refs: Romans 9:22-24; Jeremiah 18:1-10; Romans 11:23; N. T. Wright, Romans, New Interpreter's Bible

echoes: Genesis 18:10; Genesis 21:12; Genesis 25:23; Exodus 4:21; Exodus 9:16; Exodus 33:19; Isaiah 1:9; Isaiah 8:14; Isaiah 10:22-23; Isaiah 28:16; Isaiah 29:16; Isaiah 45:9; Jeremiah 18:1-12; Malachi 1:2-3; Galatians 4:21-31; Romans 3:1-4; Romans 8:28-30; Romans 11:1-36

settings.what: Paul's argument about Israel and God's faithfulness
settings.by: Paul, writing through the scribe Tertius (16:22)
settings.to: The believers in Rome: a mixed church of Jews and Gentiles meeting in several house churches, with Gentiles now in the majority (11:13). Paul had not visited them (1:10-13).
settings.when: In the winter of about AD 56-57, from Corinth, before Paul carries the collection to Jerusalem (15:25-31). Some date the letter a year or two earlier or later.
settings.why: Paul has just said that nothing can separate believers from the love of God (8:38-39). A Jewish reader will ask at once: what then of God's promises to Israel, most of whom have not believed? If God can drop Israel, why trust him with the church? Paul answers that God's word has not failed (9:6), that Israel's unbelief is not final (11:11), and that Gentile believers owe their place to Israel's root (11:18). He also speaks to Gentile pride in the Roman churches (11:13-25) and clears himself of the charge that he teaches against his own people (compare Acts 21:21).
settings.readers: Gentile believers who had heard that the church had replaced Israel, and Jewish believers who feared that they were being pushed aside. The long argument is for both.
views: The main purpose is to stop the Gentile majority in Rome from despising Jews and Jewish believers (11:18, 20, 25). Chapter 9 and 10 build up to that warning.
The main purpose is theological: to show that God's word has not failed (9:6) in a gospel that Israel has largely not accepted. The Gentile warning is a result, not the goal.
A defense of Paul's own mission
Paul is about to take the collection to Jerusalem and expects trouble (15:31). The chapters show him as a loyal Israelite so that the Roman church can stand with him.

settings.what: The word to Rebecca and the word of Malachi
settings.by: The LORD, in Genesis 25:23 and Malachi 1:2-3, as Paul quotes him
settings.to: In Genesis: Rebecca, pregnant with twins and asking the LORD why they struggled inside her. In Malachi: the people of Judah after the exile, who asked how God had loved them (Malachi 1:2). In Paul: the believers in Rome.
settings.when: Genesis: the age of the patriarchs, before the twins were born. Malachi: after the exile. Paul: the 50s AD.
settings.why: To Rebecca the word told what her two sons would become, two peoples, one serving the other. To Judah in Malachi, "I loved Jacob" answered the doubt about God's love by pointing to Edom's ruin. Paul puts the two together to show that God's purpose rests on his call and not on birth order or deeds.

settings.what: God's words to Moses and to Pharaoh
settings.by: The LORD, in Exodus 33:19 and Exodus 9:16, as Paul quotes him
settings.to: In Exodus 33:19: Moses, after the golden calf, asking to see God's glory. In Exodus 9:16: Pharaoh, through Moses, during the plague of hail. In Paul: the believers in Rome, and the imagined objector of 9:14.
settings.when: Exodus: the wilderness and the plagues, in the story's own order. Paul: the 50s AD.
settings.why: Moses heard the words as God's answer to a plea for a people that had sinned; Pharaoh heard them as notice that he had been kept alive for a purpose. Paul sets the two side by side to show that both mercy and hardening belong to God's freedom.

settings.to: An imagined objector addressed as "human being" (9:20). The objector is a rhetorical figure, not a particular Jew or Gentile in Rome.
settings.when: In the middle of the argument, in the style of a classroom debate (diatribe).
settings.why: To keep the reader from turning the argument into a trial of God. The answer is not a proof that the outcome is fair by human measure but a reminder that the one asking is a creature questioning his maker, as Israel did in Isaiah 29:16 and 45:9.
views: Most scholars (Stowers, Moo, Dunn) take the objector as a teaching device common in ancient debate, not as a real person.
Some hear a Jewish objector who protests that God is blaming Israel for what he had planned; the Isaiah texts were spoken to Israel.
A few hear a Gentile who has been told that Israel was cast off, and now asks why God still holds people to account.

settings.what: Hosea's words, as Paul quotes them
settings.by: The prophet Hosea, in the northern kingdom of Israel in the 700s BC, as quoted by Paul
settings.to: In Hosea: the northern kingdom, whose children were named Not-loved and Not-my-people to announce that God had broken with it. In Paul: the believers in Rome, who are told that those called "my people" now include Gentiles.
settings.when: In Hosea, before the Assyrian conquest of the north (722 BC). In Paul, the 50s AD.
settings.why: In Hosea, the reversal of the names promises that disowned Israel will be taken back. Paul uses it to show that God's calling of people who were "not my people" fits what God has always done.

settings.by: The prophet Isaiah, as quoted by Paul
settings.to: In Isaiah: the people of Judah and Jerusalem in the late 700s BC, under Assyrian threat (Isaiah 1:7-9; 10:20-23). In Paul: the Roman believers.
settings.when: In Isaiah, about 701 BC, when Assyria laid waste Judah and Jerusalem barely survived. In Paul, the 50s AD.
settings.why: In Isaiah the survivors are proof that God has not ended his people. Paul uses the same texts to say that Israel's present smallness in the church is not new and does not mean the promise has failed.

traditions.q: Does Romans 9 teach that God chooses individuals for salvation before they are born?
views: Yes. God chose a definite number of persons for eternal life before the foundation of the world, not because of anything he foresaw in them, and passed over the rest. The Westminster Confession (ch. 3) and the Canons of Dort (head 1) cite Romans 9:11-23; Calvin (Institutes 3.21-24) reads Jacob and Esau as persons. Barth, within the Reformed tradition, taught a different form: Jesus Christ is the one elected and rejected, and all other election is in him (Church Dogmatics II/2).

God elects those who are saved, "in Christ," and the whole cause of salvation is his grace. The Formula of Concord (Solid Declaration XI) rejects the teaching that God has decreed some people to be lost: those who perish perish by their own unbelief. Luther's Bondage of the Will took a stronger line on God's hidden will, and Lutherans have not agreed on how the two fit together.

God predestines to glory, and nobody is predestined to hell (Catechism 1037). Aquinas (Summa I, q. 23) holds that God's choice does not depend on foreseen merit, and the Council of Trent warns against presuming on one's own election (session 6, ch. 12). Within the Church the Thomist and Molinist schools disagree about how God's choice and human freedom fit together, and the Church has not settled between them.

God foreknows all and wills the salvation of all; election is not a decree that cancels human freedom. Orthodox writers such as Chrysostom read Romans 9 as speaking of God's patience and of Israel's history. The East has generally not followed Augustine's teaching on predestination, holding that God and the human will work together (synergeia).

Article 17 says that predestination to life is God's eternal purpose, secret to us, and it warns that curious people who look into God's decrees can be led to despair; it calls for looking at election in Christ. Anglicans have held both Calvinist and Arminian readings.

Election is God's choice, in Christ, of those who believe; Wesley held that God's foreknowledge does not cause anyone's fate and that Romans 9 concerns God's choice of peoples and roles (Predestination Calmly Considered; Free Grace). Wesley rejected unconditional election.

Baptists are divided. Particular (Calvinist) Baptists hold the teaching of the 1689 Confession (ch. 3) that God chose some persons unconditionally; General Baptists and many Southern Baptists teach that election is God's gracious purpose "consistent with the free agency of man" (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 5).

traditions.q: Who hardened Pharaoh, and does God harden people today?
views: God hardens those whom he does not choose to soften, and he does so justly, because those hardened are already guilty. Calvin treats it as God's active judgment, using the sinner's own will; Pharaoh is an example of a person passed over (Institutes 2.4; 3.24).

God's hardening is real and judicial: when people keep refusing, God hands them over. The Formula of Concord (Solid Declaration XI) holds that God is not the cause of anyone's sin or rejection; Pharaoh hardened himself first, and God then confirmed it.

Aquinas teaches that God withholds the grace that would soften a heart that has chosen to refuse it; he does not put evil into the heart (Summa I, q. 23, a. 3; I-II, q. 79). Hardening is permission, not authorship.

Origen's image of the sun that melts wax and hardens clay is widely cited in the East: the same divine action softens or hardens depending on the heart (On First Principles 3.1.10). Chrysostom reads Pharaoh as a man whom God's patience failed to move.
Wesley and Arminius hold that Pharaoh first hardened himself, as the early plagues in Exodus show, and that God's hardening is a judgment on a man who refused to turn.

traditions.q: If mercy "does not depend on the one who wills," is the human will free?
views: The will is not free to choose God without being changed by grace first; Romans 9:16 shows that the first move is God's (Luther, Bondage of the Will; Westminster Confession ch. 9).
The will is wounded but not destroyed; grace comes first and the will freely cooperates (Trent, session 6, ch. 5, and canons 4-5). Romans 9:16 means that human effort alone does not earn salvation.
God's grace and the human will work together; the first move belongs to God, and the will's freedom to say yes or no is real. Romans 9:16 excludes boasting, not co-working.
Prevenient grace given to all restores enough freedom that a person can accept or refuse; no one earns it, so Romans 9:16 is not violated.

The Church is the new people of God and Israel's heir, but God does not take back his gifts to the Jewish people (Romans 11:29). Nostra Aetate 4 says that the Jews remain most dear to God; the Catechism (839-840) calls the Jewish people the first to hear God's word. Lumen Gentium 9 and 16 describe the Church as the new people of God and the Jews as chosen first.

There is one people of God in all ages and one covenant of grace; the Church is the continuation of Israel, and believing Gentiles are children of Abraham (Westminster Confession 7 and 25; Calvin, Institutes 2.10-11). Romans 9:6 distinguishes the true Israel within Israel.

Lutherans have mostly read Romans 9:6 as separating believing Israel from Israel by birth; no confession addresses the verse, so this is stated as commonly taught. The Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (1994) rejected Luther's attacks on the Jews and opposed anti-Semitism in a declaration to the Jewish community; the declaration does not itself speak of covenant.
The Church is the new Israel; the fathers (Justin, Chrysostom) speak of Christians as the true Israel.
Israel and the Church are distinct. God's promises to national Israel, including land and kingdom, stay to be fulfilled, and Romans 9-11 is the proof text (Scofield).

Jews remain Israel by God's covenant, and Jewish believers in Jesus are the remnant (11:5) that continues to live as Jews. Gentile believers are joined to Israel (11:17), not a new Israel beside it (Kinzer).

The Seventh-day Adventist Fundamental Beliefs describe the church as continuing the people of God of Old Testament times. Adventist writers have commonly called the church "spiritual Israel," made up of all believers, Jew or Gentile, who are Abraham's offspring (Galatians 3:29); that wording is commonly taught and is not in the belief statement.

title: The Word Is Near You
sum: Paul turns from God's choosing to Israel's response. His heart's desire is that Israel be saved, but he must say that their zeal is not guided by knowledge: they did not know God's righteousness, tried to set up their own, and did not submit to God's (10:1-3). He says that Christ is the end of the law for everyone who believes (10:4), and he sets two ways of speaking side by side: Moses on the righteousness that comes from the law (Leviticus 18:5), and the righteousness that comes from faith, which speaks in words borrowed from Deuteronomy 30 (10:5-8).

The center of the chapter is the confession "Jesus is Lord" and the belief that God raised him from the dead (10:9-10), with the promise that anyone at all who calls on the Lord's name will be saved, Jew or Greek (10:11-13). Then comes a chain of questions: how can they call, believe, hear, proclaim, unless they are sent? (10:14-15). Paul proves from the Scriptures that Israel heard and did not all obey, while those who were not looking found God (10:16-21). The chapter ends with God's hands stretched out all day long to a disobedient people.
readings: Read as a plea for Israel

The chapter begins and ends with Israel: Paul prays for their salvation (10:1) and closes with God's open hands (10:21). Read this way, the confession of 10:9 is an invitation to his own people, the same one he gives to everyone, and the quotations from Moses and Isaiah show that God has been calling Israel through its own Scriptures all along.
Read as an argument about the law

The center of the chapter is Paul's use of Moses. Leviticus 18:5 and Deuteronomy 30:12-14 appear side by side, and 10:4 says Christ is the end (telos) of the law. The traditional Protestant reading finds here the contrast of law and gospel; the New Perspective finds a contrast between Israel's national hold on the law and the open door of faith; Jewish readers ask what Paul can mean by "end" without saying the Torah has stopped being Torah.
Read as a charter for mission

Verses 14 to 15 are among the most-quoted passages on missions: nobody can believe without hearing, hear without a preacher, or preach without being sent. They have been read as a command to the church for every age. In their setting they answer a narrower question: has Israel had the chance to hear? Paul's reply is that the message has gone out into the whole world (10:18).

views.H: In the 50s the readings of Moses and the Prophets were familiar to Jews in Rome's synagogues, and Gentile God-fearers knew them as well. The confession "Jesus is Lord" belongs to the worship of the early house churches, where it stood against "Caesar is Lord." Paul's field of work, from Jerusalem round to Illyricum (15:19), is the world he has in mind in 10:18. The Jewish people of the empire were scattered across the Mediterranean, so the gospel's reach also meant its reach to the synagogues.
views.C: 10:4 and 10:5-8 are the most debated verses: the sense of telos, the relation of Leviticus 18:5 to Deuteronomy 30:12-14, and Paul's way of quoting with "that is" (a method like the Qumran commentaries, or an application of the text to Christ). There are variants at 10:1, 5, 9, 15 and 17. Some see in 10:9-10 a pre-Pauline confession or a baptismal formula (Käsemann); that is a conjecture that cannot be tested. Whether 10:14-15 is about Israel or about all peoples is debated.
views.L: The chapter is a web of quotations: Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Joel, Isaiah, Psalm 19, Deuteronomy 32, Isaiah 65. The chain "call, believe, hear, proclaim, send" in 10:14-15 is a sorites, a ladder of steps in reasoning, and each Isaiah quotation is a witness. The diatribe questions return in 10:18 and 10:19 ("Did they not hear?" "Did Israel not know?"). The word rhema, "word" or "saying," runs through 10:8, 17 and 18.
views.J: Deuteronomy 30 is the Torah's own promise of return and repentance, and in Jewish tradition it is a reminder that the commandment is within reach: "It is not in heaven" (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59b). Paul's claim that this "word" is Christ is a Christian claim, and a Jewish reader may say that it reads Christ into a text about the commandment. Paul-within-Judaism scholars (Nanos, Gager) point out that Paul is writing to Gentiles when he says Christ is the end of the law. Jewish readers of Isaiah 65:1-2 hear the LORD's own hands stretched out to Israel.
views.T: The Reformers took 10:4 as the end of the law as a way to righteousness (Luther, Preface to Romans) and 10:17 as the foundation of preaching (Second Helvetic Confession, ch. 1). Aquinas and Catholic teaching see in Christ the fulfillment of the law, with its moral commands continuing (Summa I-II, q. 107). Catholic and Orthodox writers cite 10:14-15 for the sending of the apostles and their successors. 10:9, with its confession, has been used in baptismal liturgies; how far confession is part of being saved is argued among the churches (see the card below).

deep.h: Two ways of speaking: Leviticus and Deuteronomy
deep.b:
Paul does not say that Moses is wrong. He says that Moses "writes" the righteousness that comes from the law in Leviticus 18:5 and that "the righteousness that comes from faith" speaks in the words of Deuteronomy 30. Both are Moses. The question is how the two relate. If the first is the law's demand and the second the gospel, as Luther and the Reformed tradition read, then the passage is a contrast between doing and believing. If, as Hays and Wright argue, Paul reads Deuteronomy 30 as the Torah's own promise of a restored heart and a nearness that only the Messiah brings, the contrast is within the Torah's story: Leviticus names the way of life Israel was given; Deuteronomy names its end. Jewish tradition reads "he will live by them" as life, not death, under the commandments (Yoma 85b; Sanhedrin 74a) and the nearness of the word (Deuteronomy 30:14) as meaning that the Torah is for the living community to apply.

The words "in your mouth and in your heart" in 10:8 prepare for the two parts of 10:9-10, mouth and heart. Paul has taken a text about doing the commandment and turned it into a text about confessing and believing. Whether that is a faithful reading or a new one is exactly what Christians and Jews have debated.

deep.h: "Jesus is Lord": a confession in three worlds
deep.b:
The short confession lived in three worlds at once. In the synagogue world, "Lord" (kyrios) was how Greek readers said the divine name, so the phrase could not be spoken lightly. In the Roman world, "Lord" was a title for the emperor, and a Christian who said "Jesus is Lord" in public risked being heard as rejecting Caesar. In the worship of the house churches, it was probably said at baptism and at the Lord's Supper (1 Corinthians 12:3; 16:22). The verse 10:13 makes the link to the divine name explicit by applying Joel 2:32 to Jesus.

Notice that Paul puts the confession next to the belief in the resurrection and calls both necessary (10:9). He does not set faith against confession: 10:10 gives each a result, righteousness and salvation. The churches differ on how the two relate to baptism and works (see the card below). Notice also what is not said: the passage does not give a formula to say. It describes the faith of a community that already confesses.

deep.h: Did Israel hear? The steps of 10:14-21
deep.b:
The chain of 10:14-15 works backwards from salvation: calling needs belief; belief needs hearing; hearing needs a proclaimer; proclaiming needs a sender. Then Paul asks the question the chain raises: have they not heard? He answers with Psalm 19:4: the voice has gone out. He asks next: did Israel not know? and replies with Deuteronomy 32:21 and Isaiah 65:1: Moses and Isaiah said in advance that God would reach those who were not looking, and that Israel would be made jealous. Finally, Isaiah 65:2: even then, God held out his hands "all day long" to a people who talk back.

The argument admits that Israel has heard and not all obeyed (10:16), and it leaves the reason to God's own saving plan, which chapter 11 will unfold. Paul does not blame Israel without also saying that the Gentiles' finding is Israel's provocation, and that the hands are still out.

echoes: Leviticus 18:5; Deuteronomy 30:1-14; Deuteronomy 32:21; Joel 2:32; Psalm 19:4; Isaiah 28:16; Isaiah 52:7; Isaiah 53:1; Isaiah 65:1-2; Acts 2:21; Acts 22:3; Galatians 3:12; Philippians 3:6-9; Romans 3:21-31; Romans 9:30-33; Romans 11:11-14

settings.to: The believers in Rome, Jewish and Gentile, who hear Israel spoken of as "them."
settings.when: As the letter is read aloud in the house churches, in the late 50s.
settings.why: To show both groups that Paul's sharp words about Israel come from a prayer and not from contempt. Zeal without knowledge is something he knew from the inside (Philippians 3:6).

settings.what: Moses' two texts: Leviticus 18:5 and Deuteronomy 30:12-14
settings.by: Moses, in the books Paul quotes; Paul applies them
settings.to: In Leviticus: the Israelites at Sinai and the resident foreigners among them, who are told to keep the rules and rulings. In Deuteronomy: all Israel on the plains of Moab, just before entering the land, with a promise of return after exile. In Paul: the believers in Rome.
settings.when: Leviticus: in the wilderness after Sinai. Deuteronomy: the last speeches of Moses, in the plains of Moab.
settings.why: In Leviticus the verse urges Israel to live apart from the practices of Egypt and Canaan. In Deuteronomy the nearness of the word reassures a people who fear that the command is too hard. Paul reads them as two voices in one Torah and uses them to show how Christ and faith answer Israel's story. For Gentile believers, he insists that the word is near them too (10:12-13).
settings.readers: Roman believers, Jewish and Gentile. The Mosaic law bound Israel (and the resident foreigner in some cases); Paul does not say that Gentile believers were ever under it (compare Romans 6:14; Galatians 2:3-5).
views: The traditional Protestant reading: Leviticus describes the law's demand, which no one meets; Deuteronomy, in Paul's hands, describes the gift of faith.
Hays and Wright: both quotations are Torah; Leviticus names Israel's life under the covenant, Deuteronomy its promised restoration, and Paul reads both as pointing to the Messiah.
Gager, Nanos: Paul is speaking to Gentiles and is not describing how Jews should relate to the Torah.

settings.to: The believers in Rome, Jewish and Gentile (note "Jew and Greek," 10:12).
settings.when: As the letter is read aloud in the house churches; the confession belongs to their worship and probably to baptism.
settings.why: To tell both groups that they stand on the same ground: one Lord, one confession, one promise. For the Jewish believers it says that they do not need anything more; for the Gentile believers it says that they need nothing less.

settings.what: The chain of questions: call, believe, hear, proclaim, send
settings.to: The believers in Rome, Jewish and Gentile. The questions answer an unspoken one: has Israel had its chance to hear?
settings.when: As the letter is read aloud in the house churches; the Isaiah line at the end is from the prophet's own time.
settings.why: Paul works backward from calling on the Lord to being sent, to show that Israel's lack of faith cannot be put down to a lack of messengers. The chain has often been read as a command to the church for mission, which it later became, but in its setting it answers a question about Israel (see 10:18).

settings.what: Moses and Isaiah on Israel's response
settings.by: Moses (Deuteronomy 32) and Isaiah (Isaiah 65), as Paul quotes them
settings.to: In Deuteronomy 32: Israel, as the Song of Moses taught it to the people to be a witness against them. In Isaiah 65: a people described as rebellious, in the exile or after it, a date debated. In Paul: the Roman believers.
settings.when: The Song of Moses is set just before Moses' death on the plains of Moab. The date of Isaiah 65 depends on the view of Isaiah (eighth century or after the exile).
settings.why: Paul uses the two witnesses to show that Israel's disobedience and the Gentiles' finding God were both foretold. They are meant to bring Israel to ask why God is reaching the nations, and to remind the Gentiles that Israel's story came first.

traditions.q: Is the Law of Moses still binding on Christians if Christ is "the end of the law" (10:4)?
views: The law has three uses: it restrains sin in society, it shows people their sin and drives them to Christ, and for the believer it guides life. Christ is the end of the law as a way to righteousness (Formula of Concord VI; Luther, Preface to Romans). The ceremonial and civil laws of Israel do not bind Christians.

The moral law, summarized in the Ten Commandments, still binds believers as a rule of life; the ceremonial laws have been fulfilled in Christ and the civil laws expired with Israel as a nation (Westminster Confession ch. 19; Calvin, Institutes 2.7-8).

Article 7 of the Thirty-Nine Articles says that the ceremonies and rites of the Old Law do not bind Christians and its civil precepts need not be received in any commonwealth, but that no Christian is free from obedience to the commandments called moral.

The Old Law is fulfilled in Christ; its moral precepts, summarized in the Ten Commandments, remain in force, while its ceremonial and judicial precepts are no longer binding (Aquinas, Summa I-II, qq. 98-108; Catechism 1961-1964).

Christ fulfilled the law and the prophets, and the Old Testament is read in the light of the Gospel. The Orthodox Church does not require Christians to keep the ceremonial law (stated as commonly taught; Ware describes the Church's life in general and does not rule on 10:4).
The law ended as a rule for the Church with the cross; believers live under grace. The law remains in force for Israel in its own dispensation and in the future kingdom (Scofield).

The law is Israel's covenant way of life and remains binding on Jews who follow Jesus. For Gentile believers it is not required (Acts 15), and Christ is the "goal" of the law (10:4) not its abolition.

The Fundamental Beliefs hold that the Ten Commandments, including the seventh-day Sabbath, remain binding on Christians. The teaching that Christ ended the ceremonial laws, which were shadows fulfilled in him, is commonly taught and is not in the belief statement.

traditions.q: Is a spoken confession part of how a person is saved (10:9-10)?
views: Salvation is by faith in Christ alone. Confession with the mouth is the open expression of a faith already given in the heart, and it comes before baptism by immersion, which pictures that faith (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, articles 4 and 7).

Faith is necessary for salvation (Catechism 161), and the Church professes it aloud in the Creed and at baptism. The believer must also confess the faith publicly (Catechism 1816). Faith is received and lived in the sacraments.

Faith is the gift of the Spirit, and justification is by faith alone (Augsburg Confession IV). The mouth's confession is the fruit of the heart's faith and is spoken in worship and in baptism (Small Catechism).

The faith is confessed in the Creed at baptism, and the baptized stand in the Church's confession. Saving faith is lived in the Church's whole life of worship and the sacraments (stated as commonly taught; Ware describes this life in general).

Faith, repentance, confession and baptism all belong to the response to the gospel. Alexander Campbell and the Churches of Christ teach that the "good confession" precedes baptism, which is for the forgiveness of sins (Campbell, The Christian System).

The Assemblies of God statement of Fundamental Truths teaches that salvation is received through repentance and faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. Many Pentecostal churches also invite people to pray aloud to receive Christ; that practice is common and is not in the statement.

title: Has God Rejected His People?
sum: Paul asks the question outright: has God rejected his people? By no means. Paul is himself an Israelite. As in Elijah's day, God has kept a remnant, chosen by grace, and the rest were hardened in words from Deuteronomy, Isaiah and the Psalms (11:1-10). But a stumble is not a fall. Through Israel's trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, and the Gentiles' blessing is meant to make Israel jealous, so that its acceptance will be like life from the dead (11:11-15).

Paul warns Gentile believers with the picture of an olive tree. Branches were broken off and wild branches grafted in, but the root holds the new branches up, and God can graft the natural branches back (11:16-24). Then he tells a mystery: a hardening has come on part of Israel until the full number of the Gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved (11:25-27). The gifts and the call of God are not taken back (11:28-29). God has shut everyone up in disobedience to show mercy to everyone (11:30-32), and Paul breaks into praise (11:33-36).
readings: Read as a promise for Israel's future

Most commentators hear in 11:25-29 a promise that the Jewish people as a whole will come to faith or be saved, in God's time, and that this promise is secure because God does not take back his gifts. Paul's own life is the first sign (11:1), his Gentile mission the means (11:13-14), and the end is the life from the dead of 11:15.
Read as a warning to Gentile Christians

The center of the chapter is the olive tree (11:16-24), addressed to a Gentile who boasts. On this reading Paul's main point is not a timetable but humility: you stand by faith, the root holds you, and the branches that were cut off are your elders. The chapter's lesson for the church is not to look down on Israel, an instruction churches often ignored.
Read as the church's story of itself

Christian readers have used chapter 11 to say who the church is. Some have said that the church is Israel's replacement. Others have said that Gentile believers are guests grafted into a tree that is still Israel's. How a church reads 11:17-24 and 11:25-29 shapes how it speaks of Jews and Judaism, which is why the chapter is a main text in the Jewish-Christian dialogue.

views.H: The warning to the Gentile branch makes best sense in a church where Gentiles outnumbered Jews and may have looked down on Jewish believers, perhaps after the expulsion under Claudius (about AD 49) and the return of Jews after 54 (Acts 18:2). The olive tree was the common tree of the Mediterranean, and every Roman villa knew grafting. Paul's own plan to go to Jerusalem and then to Spain (15:24-28) stands in the background: a man who is about to ask for help for the poor in Jerusalem tells Rome to honor Israel.
views.C: Most take 11:25-27 as Paul's own composition; a few see a received apocalyptic saying behind it, an idea that cannot be tested. The Greek of 11:25 ("in part," "until") and 11:26 ("and so") gives the main cruxes. Variants at 11:6, 13, 21 and 31 change the English slightly. The quotations in 11:26-27 blend Isaiah 59:20-21, Isaiah 27:9 and perhaps Jeremiah 31:33-34, and depart from both the Hebrew and the Septuagint.
views.L: Chapter 11 returns in order to the questions of chapters 9 and 10: "God's word has failed?" (9:6) becomes "did God push his people away?" (11:1). The section 11:30-32 closes the circle of mercy that opened at 9:15-23, and the doxology answers the objector of 9:19-20 with praise. The olive tree is the longest metaphor in the letter. Pairs run through the chapter: stumble and fall, broken off and grafted in, kindness and severity, disobedience and mercy, from and through and to.
views.J: 11:1-2 and 11:28-29 are among the most-cited verses in Jewish-Christian dialogue. Jewish readers note that Paul still says "Israel" for the people and never says it has been replaced; they also note that the hope of 11:26 is stated in terms of Christ. Fredriksen and Nanos read the chapter as a Jewish apostle telling Gentile believers not to boast and to honor Israel. Others see in it a hope that Jews will become Christians. The Sonderweg question (Israel saved by a separate path) is discussed in the note on 11:26.
views.T: From Chrysostom to the Reformation most Christians took 11:25-26 to mean that the Jews would be converted before the end, though Calvin read "all Israel" as the whole church of Jews and Gentiles. The same churches often taught that Jews as a people had been displaced, and Augustine's idea of the Jews as "witness people" (City of God 18.46) kept them in a subordinate place. After the Holocaust Barth (Church Dogmatics II/2), Nostra Aetate 4, and later statements by Lutheran, Reformed and other churches returned to 11:17-29. Catholic teaching also looks to the end, when "all Israel" will be saved (Catechism 674); dispensationalists read the chapter as the restoration of national Israel.

deep.h: Supersessionism: a short and honest history
deep.b:
What the word means. Supersessionism (from Latin supersedere, "to sit above, to replace") is the view that the church has taken the place of Israel in God's plan, so that God's promises to Israel now belong to the church and the Jewish people no longer have a special place. R. Kendall Soulen distinguishes three forms: punitive (God has cast off Israel as a punishment for rejecting or killing Jesus), economic (Israel had a temporary role in preparing for Christ and is not needed after him), and structural (the Christian story is told so that Israel does nothing after the Old Testament that the church does not do better). A reader may reject the first and still find the third in the way the Bible is read.

The strongest case for fulfillment. Not everything that has been called supersessionism is punitive, and its best defenders do not begin in contempt for Jews. The one-covenant reading of Reformed theology holds that there is one people of God in all ages, so the church continues Israel and believing Gentiles are children of Abraham (Westminster Confession 7 and 25; Calvin, Institutes 2.10-11). Catholic teaching calls the church the new people of God (Lumen Gentium 9) while holding that the Jews remain most dear to God (Nostra Aetate 4). The fathers who called Christians the true Israel (Justin) read the promises as fulfilled in Christ and open to all, and pointed to Galatians 6:16, Philippians 3:3, Ephesians 2:11-22, 1 Peter 2:9-10 and Hebrews 8. None of these says Israel has no place; they say its promises find their yes in Christ (compare 2 Corinthians 1:20). Soulen's distinction matters here: "fulfillment and expansion" is one claim, and "punitive replacement" another.

How it grew. From early on Christians read the Old Testament as theirs. The Epistle of Barnabas (about AD 100-130) says that the covenant is "ours" and reads Genesis 25:23, "the elder will serve the younger," as the church overtaking Israel. Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho, about 155-160) calls Christians the true Israel. Tertullian (An Answer to the Jews) reads the same verse of Jews serving Christians. Melito of Sardis (about 170) charged Israel with killing God. In 386-387 John Chrysostom preached eight sermons in Antioch against Christians who were keeping Jewish festivals, in language of savage contempt for Jews. Augustine took a different line: Jews should not be killed or forced to convert, because they are scattered as living witnesses to the Scriptures (City of God 18.46, on Psalm 59:11); this protected them and kept them subordinate. In the Middle Ages these ideas were joined to laws, expulsions and massacres. Luther's On the Jews and Their Lies (1543), written after he had hoped for Jewish conversions, is one of the worst. Reformed covenant theology, with its one covenant of grace, treated the church as Israel's continuation, which is a different claim from the punitive one, and also expected, in many writers, a future turning of the Jews (11:26).

What changed. After the Holocaust many Christians asked how much the church's teaching had prepared the ground. The Seelisberg conference (1947) issued ten points; Jules Isaac's work on Jesus and Israel (1948) had pressed the question; Karl Barth's doctrine of election gave Israel a permanent place (Church Dogmatics II/2); the Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate 4 (1965) cited Romans 11:28-29 and rejected the charge of collective guilt; Rosemary Ruether's Faith and Fratricide (1974) argued that the roots of anti-Jewish teaching lay in Christian theology itself; John Paul II spoke of the Old Covenant as never revoked (Mainz, 1980); the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (1994) disowned Luther's anti-Jewish writings; and a Vatican commission wrote that the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable (2015). Jewish statements such as Dabru Emet (2000) responded.

What Romans itself says. Paul writes: God has not rejected his people (11:1-2); the Gentile is a wild branch grafted into Israel's tree, held up by its root (11:17-18); the branches cut off can be grafted in again (11:23); "all Israel will be saved" (11:26); the gifts and call of God are not taken back (11:29). Most New Testament scholars hold that Romans 11 does not teach punitive replacement, the church taking over Israel's place because Israel was cast off. Not everyone draws the stronger conclusion: Reformed and Catholic readers of the fulfillment view (above) hold that the promises are fulfilled in Christ and shared with the nations. Yet readers who hold that salvation is only through faith in Christ say that Paul still means Israel's salvation to come through him (11:23, 26), and some call that a kind of fulfillment rather than replacement. Some Messianic Jewish writers (Kinzer) and "Paul within Judaism" scholars (Nanos, Fredriksen) go further and say that Paul has no mission to convert Jews as such. Others reply that this reading takes the verb "save" out of the sentence. The matter is live; the churches' official statements are set out in the card below.

A caution. The history above is not an accident of one century. When Romans 9-11 is read as a story of Gentile triumph, it ends in the very arrogance that 11:18-25 warns against. Whatever a reader concludes about 11:26, the warning to the Gentile branch is the one thing about this chapter on which Paul leaves no room.

deep.h: Reading chapters 9 to 11 as one argument
deep.b: Chapter 9 says God is free and has always chosen inside Abraham's family. Chapter 10 says Israel is responsible: they heard and did not all obey. Chapter 11 says God is faithful, and that Israel's stumble serves a larger purpose. Paul holds the first two side by side without resolving them, and the third rescues them: the God who chooses and the people who refuse meet in a mercy that is meant for both (11:30-32). The inclusio on "mercy" (9:15-23, 11:30-32) and the doxology (11:33-36) are the clues that Paul's aim is not to define two classes of people but to end on God's riches. Readers of every tradition can agree that the chapters end in awe, not a syllogism.

deep.title: Claude's theory: "and so" names a process, and the "now" of 11:31 shows it has begun
deep.b: My own suggestion, labeled as such: the logic of 11:11-15 and 11:30-31 shows what houtos ("and so") in 11:26 points to. The engine is the jealousy of Deuteronomy 32:21 (quoted in 10:19): Gentile mercy provokes Israel to jealousy, and Israel's return in turn proves God's mercy to the Gentiles. In 11:31 Paul says that Israel is disobedient now so that Israel may be shown mercy now, which suggests that the process is already running in Paul's own time (11:14: "save some of them"). On this reading "all Israel will be saved" names the result of a continuing process, with no date fixed, rather than a single final event, and "until" in 11:25 marks the process's limit. This overlaps with Richard Bell's study of the jealousy motif and with Cranfield's reading of the manner of Israel's salvation. It depends on the second "now" of 11:31, which some editions omit (see the variant entry), and on taking "so that" in 11:31 as I do. It is a guess; it does not decide whether "all Israel" means the whole nation, the elect, or the whole people of God.
deep.refs: Romans 10:19; Romans 11:11; Romans 11:14; Romans 11:25-26; Romans 11:30-31; Deuteronomy 32:21

echoes: 1 Kings 19:10-18; Deuteronomy 29:4; Deuteronomy 32:21; Psalm 69:22-23; Psalm 94:14; Isaiah 6:9-10; Isaiah 27:9; Isaiah 29:10; Isaiah 40:13; Isaiah 59:20-21; Jeremiah 11:16; Jeremiah 31:31-34; Job 41:11; Hosea 2:23; Numbers 15:17-21; Ephesians 2:11-22; Galatians 6:16; Romans 9:6; Romans 15:8-12

settings.by: The prophet Elijah and the LORD, as told in 1 Kings 19 and quoted by Paul
settings.to: In 1 Kings: God and Elijah alone, on Mount Horeb. In Paul: the Roman believers, who are to see in Elijah's story a pattern for their own day.
settings.when: In 1 Kings, in the ninth century BC, after Elijah fled Queen Jezebel's threat following the contest with the prophets of Baal on Carmel.
settings.why: In 1 Kings the answer corrects Elijah's loneliness: God has seven thousand who did not bow to Baal. Paul uses it to tell Rome that Israel's unbelief is never total: God keeps a remnant that is his own doing.

settings.by: Moses, Isaiah and David (the Psalm's heading), as Paul quotes them
settings.to: In Deuteronomy: Israel on the plains of Moab, just before the covenant was renewed. In Isaiah 29: the leaders and people of Jerusalem. In Psalm 69: the psalmist's enemies, in the prayer of a righteous sufferer. In Paul: the believers in Rome.
settings.when: Deuteronomy: the last speeches of Moses. Isaiah: the late 700s BC, by the usual dating. Psalm 69: a psalm credited to David. Paul: the 50s AD.
settings.why: Each source speaks of blindness or a curse falling on people who could not or would not see. Paul gathers them to explain why most of Israel has not believed, and in 11:11 he says at once that the stumble is not final.

settings.what: The warning to the Gentile branch
settings.to: "You Gentiles" (11:13), and then a single Gentile addressed as "you" in the singular (11:17-24). The singular "you" is a rhetorical figure, as the interlocutor of 2:1 and 9:19-20 is, not a named person, though it describes an attitude Paul may have heard of.
settings.when: As the letter is read aloud in the Roman house churches, in the late 50s, after the return of Jews expelled by Claudius.
settings.why: To stop Gentile believers from boasting over Jews and Jewish believers. Paul asks them to see that they depend on Israel's root, that God was not obliged to spare them, and that the branches cut off can be restored.
settings.readers: The Gentile majority in Rome's house churches, and the Jewish believers who would have heard themselves described in the broken branches and the root.
views: Gentile believers looked down on Jews and Jewish believers, perhaps after the expulsion, and Paul answers what he knows or has heard of (Dunn, Moo, Wright).
The boasting Gentile belongs to the diatribe style and does not tell us what the Roman church was like (Stowers).

settings.what: The mystery of Israel's hardening and salvation
settings.to: The Gentile believers in Rome, addressed as "brothers" (11:25), within a letter to the whole church.
settings.when: At the climax of the argument of chapters 9 to 11, before the doxology.
settings.why: To give the Gentile believers a reason not to boast: the story of Israel is not over, and their own place depends on God's mercy. The mystery is told so that they will not think they are wise on their own.
views: Most scholars take the "you" as Gentile believers and "they" as Israel (Moo, Cranfield, Dunn).
Some scholars note that the whole letter went to all of the Roman believers, Jewish and Gentile, and that Jewish believers would have been listening for what is said about their own kin.

settings.to: The believers in Rome, who would have said or heard it aloud.
settings.when: At the end of the argument of chapters 9 to 11, before the practical teaching begins at 12:1.
settings.why: To end the argument with worship. After three chapters that press God's freedom, mercy and faithfulness to the edge of what can be said, Paul stops arguing and praises. The hymn tells the reader that what is left is wonder, not a final solution to the question of Israel. The two questions in 11:34-35 come from Isaiah 40:13, where the exiles in Babylon are told that no one advised the LORD, and from God's speech in Job 41:11, where nobody can claim that God owes them.

traditions.q: Will "all Israel" be saved, and how? (11:26)
views: The Church awaits "the full inclusion of the Jews in the Messiah's salvation" at the end, when "all Israel" will be saved (Catechism 674; Romans 11:12, 15, 25-26). A reflection by the Holy See's Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews (2015), which says that it is not a magisterial or doctrinal text, states that the Church neither conducts nor supports any specific institutional mission to Jews, while affirming that God's gifts and calling to Israel are irrevocable and that Jews are saved through Christ in a way that remains a mystery of God.

Opinions differ. Calvin read "all Israel" as the whole people of God, Jews and Gentiles together. Many later Reformed and Puritan teachers (Hodge, Murray) expected a future mass turning of Jews to Christ, and the Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 191) teaches the church to pray that "the Jews [be] called, the fullness of the Gentiles brought in." Others hold that "all Israel" is the elect of Israel gathered through the age.

Luther, who had earlier hoped for Jewish conversions, turned in 1543 to savage attacks on Jews (On the Jews and Their Lies), which Lutheran bodies now repudiate. The Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (1994) rejected those attacks and opposed anti-Semitism in a declaration to the Jewish community; the declaration does not itself speak of covenant.
The Fathers (Chrysostom, Theophylact) generally expected the Jews to turn to Christ at the end of the age.

God will restore national Israel to its land and bring it to faith at the end, after the Church age; "all Israel" is the Jewish nation living at that time, saved after the Church is complete (Scofield).

"All Israel" is the Jewish people, who stay in covenant with God. Some Messianic Jews expect a national turning to Yeshua; others (Kinzer) stress that Jewish life and the Church are bound together and that the Church does not replace Israel.

traditions.q: Can a believer be "cut off" like the broken branches? (11:22)
views: The elect will persevere to the end; the warning is real, because it is the means God uses to keep them from falling (Westminster Confession ch. 17; Canons of Dort, head 5). Some Reformed readers take 11:22 as a warning to the Gentile church as a body.

A believer can fall from grace by unbelief, though God never lets go of those who hold on to his promise; Lutherans reject a doctrine of unconditional perseverance (Augsburg Confession XII; Formula of Concord XI).

A person who has received grace can lose it by mortal sin and can be restored by repentance (Trent, session 6, ch. 14-15); the final gift of perseverance cannot be earned and must be asked for (Catechism 162, 2016).
Article 16 of the Thirty-Nine Articles says that after receiving the Holy Spirit we may depart from the grace given and fall into sin, and by God's grace rise again and amend our lives.
Salvation is a lifelong path; one can leave it. The warning of 11:22 describes a real possibility, and the Church's response is repentance and the sacraments.

Believers can fall away by willful, persistent sin or unbelief, and can be restored (Wesley, Serious Thoughts upon the Perseverance of the Saints); the warning in 11:20-22 is addressed to all who stand.

Most Baptists teach that true believers persevere (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 5), and read the warning as a test of whether a profession is genuine. General Baptists teach that a believer can fall away.

traditions.q: Will God finally show mercy to everyone? (11:32)
views: God wills all to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4), but he predestines no one to hell (Catechism 1037); hell is the result of a person's final refusal. The Church teaches the reality of hell and does not teach that everyone is saved, but allows hope for all.

The Church has not made universal salvation a dogma and the Fifth Council (553) is cited against the Origenist teaching of a final restoration of all. Some Orthodox teachers, such as Gregory of Nyssa and Isaac of Nineveh, hoped for the salvation of all.

"All" in 11:32 means Jews and Gentiles as groups. Not everyone is saved: the elect are (Westminster Confession ch. 3). Barth refused to teach universal salvation yet held that God's election is for all in Christ (Church Dogmatics II/2).
God desires all to be saved (Formula of Concord XI), yet many refuse and are lost; Scripture does not allow a doctrine of final restoration.
God's mercy is offered to all and Christ died for all, but a person can refuse; Wesley opposed the idea that all will certainly be saved (Free Grace; Predestination Calmly Considered).
The offer of mercy is to all who believe; those who reject the gospel face judgment. Baptists generally reject universalism.
